root.meaning: a device made of three stakes
root.note: The TLFi and Wiktionary give this origin through a verb *tripāliāre, ‘to torture’, that no text records. Several scholars dispute the link.

history: Le travail started as pain. The oldest French uses are grim: in the Song of Roland, around 1100, travailler means to torment someone, and the noun first appears, around 1130, for the pains of childbirth. The meaning ‘effort’ came next, and ‘work’ last. Where the verb comes from is less clear. The TLFi and Wiktionary trace it to Latin tripalium, a device of three stakes, through a verb *tripaliare, ‘to torture’, which no text records. A church council at Auxerre in the 6th century mentions torture at the tripalium, but the word also seems to name a frame for holding horses and oxen still, and French farriers still call such a frame un travail. Several scholars doubt the torture story. English travel is the same word: journeys used to be hard work.
historyEinfach: In old French, travailler meant ‘to torment, to make someone suffer’. Travail was pain, for example the pain of a woman giving birth. Later it meant hard effort, and then work. Many dictionaries say the word comes from tripalium, a Latin tool with three stakes. But not all experts agree. English travel is the same word.

chain: Old French travailler ‘to trouble, to wear out’
elsewhere.text: In Middle English travaillen meant to toil. A long journey was toil, and travel split off as a word of its own. English also kept travail for hard work.
